facts: Scott J. VanBommel, Abigail L. Knight, Andrea D. Harrington, Sydney Do, Christopher D. K. Herd, Yang Liu, Jeff A. Berger, Benton C. Clark et al. published 'Fine and ultrafine Martian dust presents additional risks for future crewed missions to Mars' in Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences (PNAS) on October 26, 2026 (doi:10.1073/pnas.2620747123).
Previous Mars missions constrained the bulk geochemistry of coarser particulates (≳3 µm), leaving fine (≲2.5 µm) and ultrafine (≲0.1 µm) fractions largely uncharacterized.
Fine and ultrafine dust particles are respirable, bypassing upper respiratory defenses to penetrate deep into alveolar regions and presenting systemic toxicity risks to crews.
The authors analyzed and modeled X-ray fluorescence data acquired by the Perseverance rover to directly examine fine and ultrafine Martian dust.
The study identified dust particulates measuring as small as 100 to 200 nm resting on spacesuit material samples and calibration targets.
Compositionally, the examined fine dust is a phosphorus-, iron-, and sulfur-enriched mafic silicate.
The dust accumulated on materials analogous to the planned external layers of potential crew systems.
The authors conclude that thorough characterization of Martian dust properties in terrestrial laboratories is critical to prepare future human crews and crew support systems.
